title: JavaScript SEO: When Rendering Hides Your Content From Google
excerpt: How Google crawls, renders and indexes JavaScript pages, the mistakes that hide content and links, SSR vs CSR in plain English, and how to compare raw and rendered HTML.

content_html:
Your new site looks great in the browser. The product pages load, the filters work, the reviews appear. Then you check Google a few weeks later and half the products are missing, or they show up with a generic snippet that has nothing to do with the product. It is a classic JavaScript SEO problem.

You right-click and choose View Source, and the page is nearly empty: a header, a <div id="root"></div>, and a few script tags. Everything a visitor sees is built by JavaScript after the page loads.

Google can run JavaScript, but anything that depends on it is processed later and is easier to break. In this guide you will learn how Google handles JavaScript pages, the specific things that go wrong, the rendering options in plain English, and how to compare what you send with what Google sees. If pages are already missing from Google, start with the wider guide to why pages are not indexed as well.

How Google crawls, renders and indexes JavaScript

Google processes JavaScript pages in three phases: crawling, rendering and indexing. Its JavaScript SEO basics guide describes the flow:

  1. Crawling. Googlebot checks robots.txt, fetches the URL, and reads the raw HTML the server sends. Links found in that HTML are added to the crawl queue.
  2. Rendering. Pages that return a 200 status are queued for rendering, unless a robots meta tag or header says not to index them. When resources allow, a headless version of Chromium runs the JavaScript and builds the final page. The page can sit in that queue for seconds or longer.
  3. Indexing. Google uses the rendered HTML to index the content and to find more links.

The raw HTML is read first and the rendered version arrives later, so anything only present after rendering is a delay and a dependency. If rendering fails, times out, or is blocked, Google only has the raw HTML to work with.

Google is also not the only system reading your pages. Many other crawlers and social media link preview tools read only the raw HTML, so a title or description set by JavaScript may never reach them.

Raw HTML vs rendered HTML

These two terms come up constantly, so it helps to be precise:

  • Raw HTML (also called source or initial HTML) is what the server sends. It is what you see with View Source.
  • Rendered HTML is the page after the browser has run the JavaScript. It is what you see in the Elements panel of your browser's developer tools.

Here is a simplified example of a client-side rendered product page. The raw HTML looks like this:

<title>Shop</title>
<div id="root"></div>
<script src="/app.js"></script>

After rendering, the same page has a product title, a description, a price, reviews and links to related products. Google can see all of that only if rendering succeeds. If the raw HTML already contains the important content, rendering becomes a bonus rather than a requirement.

What goes wrong with JavaScript sites

Content that appears only after JavaScript or a click

Content built entirely in the browser depends on rendering going well. Content that loads only when someone clicks a tab, presses "Load more" or scrolls in a particular way is riskier still, because Googlebot does not click buttons or type into boxes like a visitor does.

Say a recipe site loads the ingredient list only when the "Ingredients" tab is clicked, by fetching it from an API at that moment. Google may never see the ingredients at all. If the content is in the HTML and simply hidden in a tab, that is far safer.

Put the content you want indexed in the HTML, or at least make sure it loads without any user interaction.

Links Google cannot follow

Google's link best practices are clear: it can generally only follow links that are <a> elements with an href attribute. A <span> or <div> with a click handler, or an <a> without an href, may work for visitors but will not reliably be crawled.

Single-page apps that switch views with URL fragments (/#/products) have a similar problem. Google does not treat fragment URLs as separate pages, so use real paths (/products) with the History API instead.

Pages reachable only through those script-driven links end up with no crawlable internal links pointing at them, which is the same problem described in our guide to finding and fixing orphan pages.

JavaScript changing the title, canonical or robots tag

It is fine to set the title and meta description with JavaScript, but changes to indexing signals need care:

  • Canonical tags. Google recommends setting the canonical in the HTML. If JavaScript changes it, make sure it matches the value in the original HTML rather than pointing somewhere else.
  • Meta robots. If the raw HTML says noindex, Google may skip rendering entirely. JavaScript that removes the noindex later may never run for Googlebot, so the page stays out of the index.

A common version of this bug: a single-page app ships a default noindex in its HTML shell "for safety" and relies on JavaScript to remove it on real pages. The result can be a site that never gets indexed.

Blocked JavaScript, CSS or API files

Google will not render JavaScript from files it is not allowed to fetch. If robots.txt disallows /assets/, /js/ or the API path your pages pull content from, the rendered page Google builds may be blank or broken. Check robots.txt for any rule that touches the resources your pages need.

Error pages that return a 200 status

In single-page apps, a "Product not found" view often still returns a 200 status code, because the server just sends the app shell. Google may treat it as a soft 404, or worse, index it. Google's guidance is to redirect to a URL that returns a real 404 or to add a noindex robots tag to the error view with JavaScript.

SSR, SSG and CSR in plain English

The fix for most JavaScript SEO problems is to change where the HTML gets built. These are the main options, using the terms from Google's rendering on the web overview:

ApproachWhere the HTML is builtSEO riskGood fit for
Client-side rendering (CSR)In the visitor's browser, by JavaScriptHighest: content depends on renderingLogged-in dashboards and app screens that do not need to rank
Server-side rendering (SSR)On the server, for each requestLow: content is in the raw HTMLPages with frequently changing content, such as stock levels
Static rendering (SSG)Ahead of time, when the site is builtLow: content is in the raw HTMLBlogs, docs, service pages and marketing pages

For pages you want to rank, send the main content, links and metadata in the raw HTML through SSR or static rendering. Most modern frameworks support this, often with JavaScript taking over afterwards to make the page interactive.

You may also read about dynamic rendering, which serves pre-rendered HTML to bots and the normal app to users. Google now calls dynamic rendering a workaround rather than a recommended solution, so treat it as a stopgap, not a plan.

Heavy client-side JavaScript has a performance cost too: it keeps the browser busy and can hurt responsiveness, which shows up in your Core Web Vitals scores.

How to compare raw and rendered HTML

You do not need to be a developer to spot the big problems. Work through these checks on one important page of each type (home, category, product or service, article):

  1. View Source vs Inspect. Open View Source and search for a sentence from the main content. Then open the Elements panel in developer tools and search again. If the sentence only appears in the second, that content depends on JavaScript.
  2. Turn JavaScript off. Disable JavaScript in your browser settings and reload. Whatever disappears is what Google would miss if rendering failed.
  3. URL Inspection in Search Console. Run a live test and view the tested page's HTML and screenshot. This shows what Google's renderer actually produced, plus any resources it could not load.
  4. Compare key tags. Check that the title, canonical, meta robots and internal links are the same in both versions.
  5. Check at scale with a crawl. A free desktop crawler like Scary Spider SEO can crawl with optional headless Chrome rendering and flag pages where content or links are added only by JavaScript, and where JavaScript changes the title, canonical or meta robots.

Also check the mobile version of key templates. Google indexes the mobile version of your pages, so the parity rules in our mobile-first indexing checklist apply to rendered content too.

A quick JavaScript SEO checklist

  • Main content is present in the raw HTML, or at least loads without any click, scroll or typing.
  • Every internal link is an <a href> pointing to a real URL, not a fragment or a click handler.
  • Title, meta description, canonical and meta robots are in the raw HTML and JavaScript does not contradict them.
  • No noindex in the HTML shell of pages you want indexed.
  • robots.txt does not block the scripts, styles or API endpoints your pages need.
  • Missing pages return a real 404 or carry a noindex.
  • Pages that need to rank use server-side or static rendering.

The bottom line

JavaScript SEO is mostly about one question: what is in the HTML before any JavaScript runs? Google can render JavaScript, but rendering happens later, can fail, and is skipped for blocked resources and noindexed pages. The more your important content, links and tags rely on it, the more can go wrong.

You do not have to give up a JavaScript framework. Use server-side or static rendering for pages that need to rank, use real links, keep indexing signals in the raw HTML, and regularly compare raw and rendered versions so problems surface before your traffic drops.

Your next step: pick your most important product or service page, compare View Source with the rendered page in developer tools, and run it through URL Inspection to confirm Google sees the same content your visitors do.

faqs.question: Can Google index JavaScript websites?
faqs.answer: Yes. Google renders pages with a headless version of Chromium and indexes the rendered result. Rendering happens after crawling and can be delayed or fail, so content that only exists after JavaScript runs is less reliable than content in the raw HTML.

faqs.question: Is client-side rendering bad for SEO?
faqs.answer: Not automatically, but it carries the most risk because every piece of content and every link depends on rendering. For pages you want to rank, server-side or static rendering is the safer choice. Client-side rendering is fine for logged-in or app-like screens that do not need to appear in search.

faqs.question: How do I see what Googlebot sees on my page?
faqs.answer: Use the URL Inspection tool in Search Console and run a live test, then view the tested page's HTML and screenshot. The Rich Results Test also shows rendered HTML for public URLs. Compare that with what you see in your own browser.

faqs.question: Does Google click buttons or scroll to load content?
faqs.answer: No. Google does not interact with pages the way a visitor does, so content that loads only after a click, swipe or typing may never be seen. Content that is already in the HTML but hidden in a tab or accordion is a much safer pattern.
